summary: First-generation (typical) antipsychotic used for psychotic disorders and, in specific settings, severe acute agitation. Effective, but higher risk of movement side effects (EPS) and serious reactions like tardive dyskinesia and neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
description: Fluphenazine is a dopamine-blocking antipsychotic (phenothiazine) used to treat psychosis (like schizophrenia) and, in some cases, severe acute agitation when psychosis is driving the behavior. It can be taken by mouth or as an injection, including a long-acting form for maintenance. The tradeoff: it can cause stiffness, restlessness, tremor, and other movement side effects, and it carries serious risks like tardive dyskinesia and neuroleptic malignant syndrome. In older adults with dementia-related psychosis, antipsychotics are linked with higher death rates—fluphenazine is not approved for that use.
patient_summary: Fluphenazine is a dopamine-blocking antipsychotic used for psychosis (like schizophrenia) and sometimes severe acute agitation when psychosis is the main driver. It comes as pills/liquid, a short-acting injection, and a long-acting injection. It can work, but it’s more likely than many newer antipsychotics to cause movement side effects (restlessness, stiffness, tremor) and rare but dangerous reactions like neuroleptic malignant syndrome. In older adults with dementia-related psychosis, antipsychotics increase the risk of death—this medication is not approved for that condition.

primary.context: Used to treat psychotic symptoms (hallucinations, delusions, disorganization). Some clinicians prefer second-generation antipsychotics first because fluphenazine has a higher EPS/tardive dyskinesia risk.
Short-acting IM fluphenazine may be used for severe, acute agitation when psychosis is suspected to be the main cause. After stabilization, transition to oral maintenance therapy.

off_label.context: Sometimes used for severe tics/Tourette syndrome when other options aren’t effective or tolerated, but side effect tradeoffs matter.

therapeutic_response.display: Oral: initial effects often within 1-2 weeks; LAI decanoate: 24-72 hours

routes: Subcutaneous (SUBQ) (labeling exists for some LAI products; often avoided by experts)

common_adverse_effects.incidence: Common (frequency varies by dose and patient factors)
common_adverse_effects.notes: This is the signature problem set for fluphenazine: stiffness, tremor, inner restlessness, and muscle spasms. Higher doses raise risk. Younger patients and males may be more prone to dystonia; older age increases tardive dyskinesia vulnerability.
Feels like agitation in the body—pacing, leg bouncing, unable to sit. This can be mistaken for “worsening anxiety.” It’s treatable, but you have to name it.
Sleepiness and slowed reaction time can show up early and after dose changes. This is where falls, driving risk, and work impairment can creep in.
Lightheaded when you stand up. Hydration helps, but persistent dizziness needs a plan—especially if you’re on blood pressure meds or are older.
Prolactin-related side effects can show up as libido changes, erectile/ejaculatory issues, menstrual changes, breast tenderness, galactorrhea, or gynecomastia.

serious_risks.risk: Tardive dyskinesia: abnormal involuntary movements that may be irreversible (risk increases with duration and cumulative exposure; higher risk with older age and certain comorbidities).
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS): fever, rigidity, altered mental status, autonomic instability—MEDICAL EMERGENCY.
Severe cardiac conduction problems/arrhythmias: rare but potentially life-threatening.
Blood dyscrasias (leukopenia, neutropenia, agranulocytosis): may be fatal; stop if ANC <1000/mm3 or concerning declines occur.
Cholestatic jaundice/hepatic injury: liver damage and jaundice reported; medication is contraindicated in hepatic impairment.
Rhabdomyolysis: rare but serious muscle breakdown.
Aspiration pneumonia: risk rises with age and swallowing dysfunction.
Withdrawal syndrome with abrupt cessation of high-dose oral therapy: agitation, insomnia, GI symptoms, dyskinesias, anxiety, sweating, tremor, vertigo, and rebound psychosis.

safety.black_box_warning: Elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis treated with antipsychotic drugs are at an increased risk of death. In placebo-controlled trials (modal duration ~10 weeks), death occurred in about 4.5% of drug-treated patients versus about 2.6% of placebo-treated patients, with a relative risk about 1.6 to 1.7. Causes were often cardiovascular (eg, heart failure, sudden death) or infectious (eg, pneumonia). Fluphenazine is not approved for the treatment of patients with dementia-related psychosis.

contraindications.contraindication: Hypersensitivity to fluphenazine or any component (possible cross-reactivity among phenothiazines)
Severe CNS depression, coma, or subcortical brain damage
Concurrent use in patients receiving large doses of hypnotics
Children <12 years of age (long-acting injectable decanoate only)

precautions: Movement disorders (EPS): akathisia, dystonia, parkinsonism; tardive dyskinesia may be irreversible
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS): fever, rigidity, confusion, autonomic instability—medical emergency
Cardiac conduction/arrhythmia risk: antipsychotics can alter conduction; use caution in cardiac disease
Orthostatic hypotension and falls: especially in older adults or medically fragile patients
Blood dyscrasias: leukopenia, neutropenia, agranulocytosis—monitor if risk factors
Aspiration risk: esophageal dysmotility/aspiration pneumonia risk increases with age
Catatonia: antipsychotics are not indicated for catatonia and may worsen outcomes and raise NMS risk

interactions.interactant: Alcohol and other sedatives (benzodiazepines, sleep meds, opioids, sedating antihistamines)
interactions.mechanism: Additive sedation, impaired coordination, falls, and dangerous CNS depression—especially in older adults.
interactions.action: Avoid or minimize combinations. If a combo is clinically necessary, use the lowest effective doses and monitor closely.

interactions.interactant: Anticholinergic medications (eg, benztropine, diphenhydramine; also many bladder meds, some antidepressants)
interactions.mechanism: More constipation, urinary retention, blurry vision, confusion—can tip older adults into delirium. Can also mask early movement symptoms until they’re severe.
interactions.action: Use deliberately (sometimes short-term to prevent acute dystonia with IM dosing), but don’t stack anticholinergics casually. Monitor bowel/bladder function.

interactions.interactant: Medications that prolong QT or increase arrhythmia risk
interactions.mechanism: Higher risk of dangerous rhythm problems, especially with electrolyte abnormalities or underlying heart disease.
interactions.action: Review QT-risk meds, correct electrolytes, and consider ECG monitoring in higher-risk patients.

interactions.interactant: Dopamine-blocking agents or antiemetics (eg, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine)
interactions.mechanism: EPS and tardive dyskinesia risk stacks.

interactions.interactant: CYP2D6 inhibitors (clinically relevant examples include some SSRIs like fluoxetine/paroxetine; bupropion; quinidine)
interactions.mechanism: Can increase fluphenazine exposure and side effects (EPS, sedation).
interactions.action: If combined, consider dose reduction and tighter monitoring for EPS and sedation.

interactions.interactant: Levodopa and other dopaminergic Parkinson’s meds
interactions.mechanism: Fluphenazine can blunt their effect and worsen parkinsonism.
interactions.action: Avoid when possible; if unavoidable, monitor closely for worsening motor symptoms.

monitoring_requirements.parameter: Adherence and response at every visit: symptoms, functioning, sleep, agitation, and relapse warning signs
Extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS) every visit, with a formal rating scale at least annually (or every 6 months if high risk); reassess 4 weeks after initiation and after dose changes
Tardive dyskinesia: check every visit and formally at least annually (or every 6 months if high risk)
Mental status and alertness every visit: sedation, cognition, delirium risk (especially older adults)
Fall risk assessments as clinically indicated, especially in patients ≥60 years and after dose changes
Vital signs as clinically indicated: blood pressure (including orthostatics), pulse, temperature; watch for infection symptoms (pneumonia risk in vulnerable older adults)
Weight/height/BMI: every visit for the first 6 months, then at least quarterly; consider waist circumference at baseline and annually
Fasting glucose/HbA1c: about 4 months after initiation, then annually (more often if abnormal)
Lipid panel: about 4 months after initiation, then annually (more often if abnormal)
Blood chemistries as clinically indicated: electrolytes, renal function, liver function tests, TSH (especially if symptoms suggest an issue)
CBC as clinically indicated; monitor more frequently in the first few months if low baseline WBC or history of drug-induced leukopenia/neutropenia; stop for severe neutropenia or concerning declines
Prolactin: ask about symptoms at every visit until dose is stable; check a level if symptoms occur (menstrual changes, sexual dysfunction, galactorrhea, gynecomastia)
ECG/arrhythmia risk: consider baseline and follow-up ECGs in patients with cardiac disease, QT-risk meds, or concerning symptoms (syncope, palpitations)
Therapeutic drug monitoring (optional, not routine): draw trough just before next dose if using levels to support adherence checks; dosing should be guided by clinical response rather than levels

special_populations.pregnancy: Class-level data for first-generation antipsychotics do not show a clear major increase in overall congenital malformations, but individual-drug data are more limited. Third-trimester exposure to antipsychotics can cause newborn EPS and/or withdrawal symptoms (agitation, feeding problems, abnormal muscle tone, respiratory distress, sleepiness, tremor). Tapering late in pregnancy to prevent neonatal symptoms is generally not recommended. The guiding principles: don’t discontinue effective treatment just because someone is pregnant, avoid polytherapy when possible, and use the lowest effective dose with close symptom monitoring.
special_populations.lactation: It’s not known if fluphenazine is present in human milk. Infants exposed to antipsychotics through breast milk have been reported to experience drowsiness, irritability, poor feeding, sedation, motor abnormalities, and slowed development. If breastfeeding while using an antipsychotic, monitor the infant closely—especially if premature or low birth weight, or if other sedating meds are in the mix. When starting postpartum, less-sedating agents are often preferred.
special_populations.pediatric: Not commonly used in pediatrics due to higher risk of acute dystonic reactions and prolactin-related effects. Off-label: chronic tic disorders may be treated in select cases, but this is specialist-level care with careful risk-benefit discussion and monitoring.
special_populations.geriatric: High-risk medication in adults ≥65. Avoid for behavioral problems associated with dementia or delirium unless nonpharmacologic options failed and there is risk of harm. Boxed warning: higher death risk in dementia-related psychosis; fluphenazine is not approved for that use. If used for appropriate indications (eg, schizophrenia), start low, titrate slowly, and monitor closely for orthostasis, falls, sedation, EPS, swallowing/aspiration risk, and hyponatremia/SIADH concerns.
special_populations.renal_impairment: No manufacturer-provided renal dose adjustment; dosage adjustment is usually unlikely because urinary excretion is limited. Use caution and monitor clinically; discontinue if BUN becomes abnormal.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Contraindicated by manufacturer in hepatic impairment/hepatic disease. Avoid use.

pharmacokinetics.peak_plasma: Oral: ~2.8 hours; LAI decanoate: peak effect often 48-96 hours (time to peak reported ~8-10 hours)
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Hepatic via CYP2D6 (minor substrate classification noted; clinically relevant interactions still possible)
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Limited urinary excretion; renal dose adjustment usually not needed

dosing.titration: Fluphenazine dosing depends on the goal: oral dosing for ongoing psychosis treatment, short-acting IM for severe acute agitation, and long-acting IM decanoate for maintenance when consistent adherence is critical. Use the lowest effective dose and titrate slowly, watching closely for akathisia and parkinsonism.

discontinuation.taper_guidance: If you’re stopping oral fluphenazine after long-term use, the safest move is usually a gradual taper over weeks to months—unless you’re stopping because of a serious adverse reaction. The goal is to watch for relapse early and reduce withdrawal/rebound symptoms (agitation, insomnia, anxiety, sweating, GI symptoms, dyskinesias, restlessness, tremor, vertigo, and rebound psychosis).

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Fluphenazine is a first-generation antipsychotic used to treat psychosis—most commonly {link:condition:schizophrenia:schizophrenia}. In the right setting, the short-acting injection can also be used for severe acute agitation when psychosis is likely driving the behavior. This is not a casual med. It’s powerful, it can be effective, and it comes with a real side effect load—especially movement symptoms.
items: {link:condition:schizophrenia:Psychotic disorders (eg, schizophrenia)}: Hallucinations, delusions, disorganization, agitation tied to psychosis

{link:condition:acute-agitation:Severe acute agitation} (short-acting IM hydrochloride only): When psychosis is suspected to be the primary cause and rapid control is needed, often with a plan to transition to oral maintenance once stable
off_label: {link:condition:tic-disorders:Tics/Tourette syndrome}: For severe tics in select cases when benefits outweigh the side effect risks

quotes: The paranoia backed off. I wasn’t scanning the room all the time.
The voices got quieter, like someone turned them down a few notches.
My brain felt less chaotic, more organized.
items.note: Oral fluphenazine often starts showing changes within 1-2 weeks, with continued improvement over 4-6 weeks.

quotes: It made me calmer, but also kind of heavy and slowed.
Less intense, less reactive… but also less energy.
I felt sleepy and flat at first.
items.note: Sedation and CNS slowing can impair driving, work, and reaction time—especially early on or after dose increases.

quotes: I couldn’t sit still. My body felt like it needed to move nonstop.
My muscles felt tight and stiff, like I was walking like a robot.
My hands shook and my jaw felt weird.
items.note: EPS can show up early (days to weeks) and needs fast attention—don’t “tough it out” and hope it goes away.

quotes: It worked, but I was always bargaining with side effects.
I kept asking: is this helping me live better, or just making me quieter?
I worried about the movement stuff becoming permanent.
items.note: Tardive dyskinesia can be irreversible. The goal is always the lowest effective dose and regular movement screening.

sections.intro: People describe fluphenazine in a very “this helped… but I paid for it” kind of way. Here are the common themes:

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Fluphenazine isn’t an instant “flip-the-switch” medication for psychosis, but the injectable forms can kick in faster for acute situations.
key_points: Oral: early changes may show up within 1-2 weeks, with continued improvement over 4-6 weeks
Short-acting IM (hydrochloride): used for severe acute agitation; effects are meant to be rapid compared to oral use (clinical response depends on situation and cause)
Long-acting injectable (decanoate): peak effect often 48-96 hours
Long-acting injectable (decanoate): duration roughly 4-6 weeks (varies by dose and patient)

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Fluphenazine can be effective for psychotic symptoms—especially when adherence is a challenge and the long-acting injection is used. The main clinical challenge is balancing benefit against a higher rate of movement side effects compared with many second-generation antipsychotics. In real life, “works” means fewer hallucinations/delusions, less agitation tied to psychosis, improved sleep and functioning, and fewer relapses—at the lowest dose that holds stability.
sections.clinical_details: Some experts prefer second-generation antipsychotics first due to potentially fewer extrapyramidal symptoms, with no consistent evidence that typicals are more effective overall. Fluphenazine’s long-acting injectable form is often chosen when consistent dosing is critical and relapse risk from missed oral doses is high.

Tell your clinician immediately if you develop restlessness, stiffness, tremor, jaw/neck tightness, or abnormal movements.
Stand up slowly and hydrate—orthostatic dizziness and falls can happen, especially early on.
Avoid mixing with other sedating meds unless your prescriber is coordinating it (risk of oversedation and falls).
If you have liver disease, this medication may not be an option—don’t self-start or self-adjust.

sections.heading: Side Effects

Sudden muscle spasms (acute dystonia) — neck/jaw/eyes can be involved
Dizziness or faintness when standing (orthostatic hypotension)
Sexual side effects and hormone-related effects (high prolactin: menstrual changes, galactorrhea, gynecomastia)
Constipation, dry mouth, blurry vision, urinary retention (anticholinergic effects—usually lower than some other antipsychotics, but still possible)

sections.intro: Fluphenazine has meaningful interaction risk—especially anything that increases sedation, worsens movement symptoms, affects heart rhythm, or alters metabolism through CYP2D6.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: If you’re stopping oral fluphenazine after long-term use, the safest move is usually a gradual taper over weeks to months—unless you’re stopping because of a serious adverse reaction. The goal is to watch for relapse early and reduce withdrawal/rebound symptoms (agitation, insomnia, anxiety, sweating, GI symptoms, dyskinesias, restlessness, tremor, vertigo, and rebound psychosis).
key_points: For chronic psychotic illness, switching to another antipsychotic is often preferred over stopping completely if side effects are the issue.
Oral taper: reduce gradually over weeks to months when feasible to catch early relapse and reduce withdrawal/rebound symptoms.
Withdrawal-type symptoms can happen—especially after abrupt discontinuation of higher doses (agitation, insomnia, anxiety, sweating, GI symptoms, dyskinesias, tremor, vertigo).
Long-acting injectable (LAI) decanoate: tapering is generally not needed because elimination is slow and withdrawal risk is lower, but relapse monitoring is still essential.

Switching strategies vary: cross-titration, overlap, or abrupt switch depending on relapse risk, side effects, and clinical stability—high-relapse-risk patients often need overlap until the new med is therapeutic.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Fluphenazine dosing depends on the goal: oral dosing for ongoing psychosis treatment, short-acting IM for severe acute agitation, and long-acting IM decanoate for maintenance when consistent adherence is critical. Use the lowest effective dose and titrate slowly, watching closely for akathisia and parkinsonism.

adult.psychosis_oral_initial: 2.5-10 mg/day PO in 1-2 divided doses (first-episode psychosis: consider 1-5 mg/day PO in 1-2 divided doses due to higher sensitivity to adverse effects)
adult.psychosis_oral_titration: Increase by 5 mg/day at intervals of about 1 week based on response and tolerability; monitor for akathisia and parkinsonism during titration
adult.psychosis_oral_maintenance: 5-20 mg/day PO in 1-2 divided doses; use the lowest effective maintenance dose
adult.agitation_im_titration: If needed based on severity and duration, 2.5-10 mg/day IM in divided doses every 6-8 hours
adult.agitation_im_caution: Use caution with total daily doses >10 mg/day
adult.lai_decanoate_initial: 6.25-25 mg IM once (after establishing tolerability with short-acting fluphenazine)
adult.lai_decanoate_oral_conversion: Dose estimation: for each 10 mg/day of stable oral fluphenazine, give 12.5 mg of fluphenazine decanoate
adult.lai_decanoate_oral_overlap: After the first injection, oral overlap may be used at ~one-half the daily oral dose; oral overlap may be stopped at the second injection
adult.lai_decanoate_maintenance: Typically 6.25-100 mg IM every 2-4 weeks; adjust by 6.25-12.5 mg every 2-4 weeks as needed

sections.simple_explanation: Oral fluphenazine is usually titrated weekly and then held at the lowest dose that keeps symptoms stable. The short-acting IM form is for severe acute agitation (often in emergency or inpatient settings), and once things calm down, clinicians usually transition to oral maintenance. The long-acting decanoate injection is for people who need steady coverage and struggle with daily pills—start only after proving you tolerate the medication.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Fluphenazine comes in oral forms for day-to-day treatment and injectable forms for acute control or long-term maintenance. Long-acting decanoate formulations may contain sesame seed oil.
items: Oral tablets (hydrochloride): 1 mg, 2.5 mg, 5 mg, 10 mg
Oral concentrate (hydrochloride): 5 mg/mL
Oral elixir (hydrochloride): 2.5 mg/5 mL
Short-acting injection (hydrochloride): 2.5 mg/mL
Long-acting injection (decanoate): 25 mg/mL (may contain sesame seed oil)

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Fluphenazine primarily works by blocking dopamine D2 receptors, especially in brain circuits tied to psychosis. That dopamine blockade can reduce hallucinations, delusions, and disorganization—but it’s also the reason movement side effects happen (dopamine matters in motor pathways too). Compared with some other antipsychotics, fluphenazine has relatively limited activity at histamine, muscarinic, and alpha receptors, but those pathways can still contribute to sedation, anticholinergic symptoms, and blood pressure effects.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Fluphenazine is a typical (first-generation) antipsychotic. In many modern treatment plans, second-generation antipsychotics are often preferred first because they can be easier to tolerate (especially for EPS), even if overall efficacy is similar across agents. Fluphenazine still has a place: patients who respond well to it, people who need a long-acting injectable option to prevent relapse from missed doses, or situations where clinicians are choosing based on prior response, side effect patterns, and medical comorbidities. In severe acute agitation, short-acting IM fluphenazine may be used when psychosis is suspected to be the main driver—often with a plan to stabilize quickly and transition to oral maintenance.
sections.note: Antipsychotics are not indicated for catatonia and may worsen outcomes and raise NMS risk in catatonic patients. When catatonia is suspected, management should be specialist-guided.

faqs.a: Fluphenazine is mainly used to treat psychotic disorders like schizophrenia. The short-acting IM form can also be used for severe, acute agitation when psychosis is suspected to be the main cause. There’s also a long-acting injection (decanoate) used for maintenance in people who need steady coverage and struggle with daily pills.

faqs.q: How long does fluphenazine take to work?
faqs.a: With oral fluphenazine, early changes are often noticed within 1 to 2 weeks, with continued improvement over 4 to 6 weeks. The long-acting decanoate injection can start working within about 24 to 72 hours, with strongest effect often around 48 to 96 hours.

faqs.q: What are the biggest side effects to watch for?
faqs.a: The big ones are movement side effects (EPS): restlessness (akathisia), stiffness/tremor (parkinsonism), and sudden muscle spasms (acute dystonia). Longer-term, tardive dyskinesia is the serious one because it can become permanent. Rare but dangerous: neuroleptic malignant syndrome (fever + severe rigidity + confusion + autonomic instability).

faqs.q: Is fluphenazine safe for dementia-related agitation or psychosis?
faqs.a: This is where the boxed warning matters. In older adults with dementia-related psychosis, antipsychotics are associated with a higher risk of death compared with placebo. Fluphenazine is not approved for dementia-related psychosis. If an antipsychotic is ever used in dementia, it should be only after non-drug strategies fail and there’s a serious risk of harm, and the plan should include frequent reassessment and deprescribing attempts.

faqs.q: What is akathisia and why does it matter?
faqs.a: Akathisia is inner restlessness—like your body can’t sit still. People pace, bounce legs, or feel intensely uncomfortable. It can look like “worsening anxiety” or agitation, but it’s actually a medication side effect and it’s treatable. If it shows up, tell your clinician fast.

faqs.q: What’s the difference between short-acting IM fluphenazine and the long-acting decanoate shot?
faqs.a: Short-acting IM (hydrochloride) is used for severe acute agitation and is typically part of emergency/inpatient stabilization, often with a plan to transition to oral maintenance. The long-acting decanoate injection is for ongoing maintenance—dosed every 2 to 4 weeks (sometimes every 2 weeks) after tolerability is established with short-acting fluphenazine.

faqs.q: Do I need to taper off fluphenazine?
faqs.a: If you’re stopping oral fluphenazine after long-term use, a gradual taper over weeks to months is usually advised to reduce withdrawal/rebound symptoms and catch relapse early—unless you’re stopping due to a serious adverse effect. For long-acting decanoate injections, withdrawal symptoms are less common because the medication leaves the body slowly, but relapse monitoring is still essential.

It can be. Some people feel slowed down or sleepy, especially early on or after dose increases. Sedation plus orthostatic dizziness is a recipe for falls—so it’s something clinicians watch closely, especially in older adults.

faqs.q: What should I do if I get fever and severe stiffness on fluphenazine?
faqs.a: That combination can signal neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS), which is a medical emergency. Seek emergency care immediately—especially if there’s confusion, sweating, fast heart rate, or blood pressure instability.

faqs.q: Does fluphenazine affect hormones or sexual function?
faqs.a: Yes, it can raise prolactin. That can lead to menstrual changes, decreased libido, erectile or ejaculatory problems, galactorrhea (milk discharge), or gynecomastia (breast tissue growth). If those show up, tell your clinician—there are management options.

faqs.q: What labs and monitoring do people usually need?
faqs.a: Movement screening (EPS and tardive dyskinesia) is the big one—checked every visit with formal tools at least yearly (more often if high risk). Weight and metabolic labs (glucose/HbA1c and lipids) are typically checked after a few months and then yearly. CBC is checked if there are risk factors for low white blood cells. ECG and electrolytes come into play if you have cardiac risk factors or are on QT-risk meds.

seo.description: Fluphenazine (Prolixin) is a first-generation antipsychotic used for schizophrenia/psychosis and sometimes severe acute agitation. Learn dosing (oral, IM, long-acting decanoate), movement side effects (EPS, tardive dyskinesia), NMS warning, and dementia boxed warning.
